text:
Commander night at Tom's, three-player pod: me on Edgar Markov, Alex on his Lord of the Rings Sauron deck, Tom on one of his blue-black decks. Lost it — Alex was on 1 life and I ran out of gas.

The deck did exactly what it is built to do. Low-drop vampires out of the gate, eminence minting a body every cast, and by turn three I had five vampires on an empty-ish board with only three mana spent. Tom looked at it and said "this is ridiculous". The whole table decided Markov was the problem immediately, which is the correct read and also the price of the plan. I could feel the v1.0.0 curve shift — more cheap vampires, and the board builds itself faster than it used to.

From there I ate everything. Multiple board wipes and a stack of counterspells, nearly all of it aimed at me. I was the reason the table's answers left their hands. What I liked is how fast I rebuilt after each wipe — the low curve plus the mana base meant I was back to a real board in a turn or two, every time. It genuinely felt like a wall of vampires the other two were just trying to hold back.

Elspeth, Storm Slayer came down and was targeted immediately, but before she died she doubled a couple of tokens for me and took out one of Tom's creatures. I liked that a lot — she pulled attention while the vampire board kept growing underneath.

Mistake I can name: Alex's Nazgul kept getting bigger every time the Ring tempted him, and I should have wiped them earlier instead of letting them proliferate. I saw it too late.

Bigger mistake: I did not cast Edgar himself until I had eight mana. I had not even been thinking about him. When he did land it was the finisher — Olivia's Wrath for a big X to clear a couple of blockers and chip a large creature, then swing wide with Edgar's haste and the +1/+1 counters on all of them. That got Alex to 1.

Tom was making himself the problem — Cyclonic Rift, counters, general interference — so we killed him first. Then I needed one more vampire and had nothing.

Two counters decided it. Tom countered Champion of Dusk when I was about to draw five off it and would happily have paid the five life; that was the refuel that would have closed the game. He also countered Bloodthirsty Conqueror, which is my Sanguine Bond half.

No win, but I am happy with it. Aggro midrange, took all the heat, rebuilt every time, and ran out of steam only after the third wipe plus the counter on my draw. That is the deck working.

Same night at Oliver's, second game, five-player pod: Oliver, Ryan, Tom, Alex and me. I was in seat 5. LOSS, but I was among the last players standing.

THE MULLIGAN WAS MY MISTAKE. Mulliganed once and kept a two-land hand. I knew at the time it should have gone back, and another player pointed out the mulligan was still available. Our house rule makes you discard on the second mulligan, and I kept out of stubbornness.

WHAT WORKED: Blood Artist and Bloodthirsty Conqueror landed early and drained a significant amount of life. The signature play of the night was a board wipe going off with the drain package online — eleven creatures died, every opponent lost 11, I gained 11 and assigned 11. Life totals afterwards were me around 50 and the table around 20. Throne of the God-Pharaoh was out doing damage on tapped creatures. Anointed Procession resolved and was removed the following turn. The deck genuinely went off for a stretch.

WHAT BROKE IT: Ryan's recurring artifact and enchantment removal on a card-draw engine — Anointed Procession and other permanents were picked off repeatedly. Then I ran out of steam: vampires on board, nothing in hand, and no way to rebuild after each wipe. That is the same failure mode that cost me the Saturday game against Alex, a winnable position that ran dry.

THE INTERACTION NEVER GOT CAST. Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat in my hand uncast for the entire game. My own diagnosis, in the order I thought of it: I am trigger-shy and sit on protection and removal rather than spending it; I am not tracking opponents' boards closely enough to know when the window is; and I am uncertain about correct timing.

But the fourth reason is the one that matters and it is structural rather than behavioural: my mana was spent casting vampires, so there was never open mana to hold up. Late in the game I did have open mana, but the board was only two tokens deep and Teferi's Protection did not feel worth it. Then a wipe came. A deck that cannot afford to hold up interaction is a deck that does not run interaction, whatever the list says.

Seat 5 again. My read is that the first-seat momentum advantage compounds with my mana deficit rather than just adding to it. And this pod runs heavy creature removal and heavy board wipes — both games were rebuild, wipe, rebuild, and neither of my decks generates value on the way down.

Commander night at Alex's house on Moraga Way in Orinda, Friday 28 August. Three-player pod: me, Alex, Stuart. Game two of four on the night.

Best-case opener and it did not matter. Two lands plus Sol Ring, tapped Sol Ring for a Talisman, ended turn one on four mana. Edgar down fast, Warleader's Call and the token-enters enchantments in place. Everything the deck wants from an opening hand, I had.

Then nothing. EDGAR WAS THE ONLY VAMPIRE I CAST ALL GAME. Got Alex to 12 commander damage before he assembled blockers; he closed later with an oversized threat. Stuart was on Jarad. I ran out of steam on card draw, which is the same theme as every other game with this build — it is not a new finding, it is the finding, again.

DIRECTION CHANGE, and it came out of a long conversation with Alex after the game. He reframed the deck and I think he is right.

What I have been building is swarm typal: Edgar makes tokens, tokens get buffed, everybody gets +1/+1, and I attack with an army of mediocre vampires. The recent refactor tried to fix this by converting tokens into value — Purphoros, Warleader's Call, the doublers — which is a good idea in isolation but does not change what the deck is. It is still a pile of okay vampires buffing each other into 4/4s and 5/5s, and that is not how I win at this table. I am playing to win at THIS table, now.

Alex's pitch is LORDS AND PAYOFFS instead. Get two or three vampires enormous and fast rather than an army of medium ones. Edgar already pumps everything when he enters and he has haste, so the play is to have a small number of bodies worth pumping. The tokens stop being the win condition and become the DIG ENGINE — card draw, treasure, moving through the deck fast — because the deck is full of mediocre vampires and the premium ones are what actually close games. I am not tutoring for anything specific; I just need to burn through enough of the deck to reliably find the good ones.

That argues for a mill package as a second way to dig, since we are in black with graveyard recursion available. Card draw is one way through the deck; self-mill is another, and we can be deliberate about it.

The through-line should be white-black lifegain into lifedrain, not going wide. The vampires worth building around are the ones with card draw, life drain and damage triggers — a big deathtouch body that drains when it connects is worth more than four 4/4s.

Named as keepers in the conversation: Cordial Vampire (whenever any creature dies, +1/+1 counter distributed — real payoff for a deck that makes and loses bodies) and Welcoming Vampire (card draw off small creatures entering, which is exactly what the token half produces).

THIS SUPERSEDES THE TOKEN-CONVERSION AXIS from the 25 August debrief. That direction is withdrawn — not because it was wrong mechanically, but because it was optimising the wrong deck.

Game 3 of three at Oliver's, five-player pod: Sean, Oliver, Tom, Alex, Ryan.

The other refactored deck through the statistical-analysis process, and THE
REFACTOR REALLY SHOWED. v1.0.0 had too many mediocre cheap vampires and weak
card draw, so it stalled once the initial token swarm ran out. v1.0.1 is twelve
swaps toward bigger, more impactful vampires.

Opened with a playable hand and got the token swarm going. Tom had Goblin
Sharpshooter pinging my tokens — but that fed the card-draw creatures (pay two
life, draw a card when a creature dies), so I was running my engine off his
removal.

Resolved a big threatening flyer that draws cards, brought Edgar down and
started swinging. Alex came in with his fight deck and took out some vampires,
so I pivoted, brought in Bloodletter of Aclazotz for the doubled damage and
swung lethal into Alex. Took him out. Ryan was not going to do anything and Tom
had no creatures (enchantment deck).

Then Tom tutored a two-card infinite combo and closed the game before my lethal
resolved.

Loss — but on board state Edgar was dominating. The deck hung with the table
and actually threatened lethal. It is working as intended.

PILOTING MOMENT I want to keep: I realised afterwards that during that
resolution I could have paid more life to pump the vampire faster — BBB, two
life, two life, two life while the creature was still there — and generated a
pile of extra cards off the death trigger. Tight play I missed in the moment.

The Alex read: I have been playing with Alex a lot and he has been winning
lately, so taking him out is correct from a table-position standpoint even
though it looks personal. That is board state, not grudge.

META NOTE, and I want this on the record: losing to a tutored two-card infinite
is UNSATISFYING in a way that losing to a better board is not. Edgar was clearly
the dominant force on the table. The real dimension separating a fun, skilful
pod game from a salty one is not power level — it is TWO-CARD INFINITE COMBOS
and TUTORABILITY. Those two are what separate "cool synergy deck" from "I won on
turn four with cards you have never seen because I tutored them." Worth writing
up as a pod-meta proposal.
